children: Crude oil futures settled modestly lower Friday in volatile trading after the
the release of diesel and crude inventories to ease high fuel prices and reports that Saudi Arabia is planning an offensive against Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen.

The G7 will deploy 100M barrels from emergency stocks over the next four months "with a front-loaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days," the group said in a joint statement; the G7 consists of Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the U.K., and the U.S.

Member nations of the International Energy Agency, a club of Western nations and their allies, had agreed to release 400M barrels of oil onto the market in March, but European countries—most of them net energy importers—have yet to let go of much of their reserves.

Most of the IEA release has come from the U.S., which has placed 130M barrels of crude from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve on the market since March; the SPR has 284M barrels left, its lowest level since 1982.

President Trump said after the move that he would not ban U.S. diesel exports, pulling back from earlier consideration of possible diesel export curbs and rebuffing Republican elected officials from Midwestern states who had sought limits as a way to cut fuel prices weighing on voters before the November midterm election.

Diesel prices, in particular, had spiked as wars in Russia and the Middle East disrupted refining and energy shipping; the average retail cost of diesel in the U.S. was $6.37/gal on Friday, according to AAA, slightly below recent record highs above $6.50/gal.

The move "highlights that the main stress in the energy market is ​no longer crude availability, with Middle East flows recovering, but rather refined product supply, constrained by reduced refinery capacity and output across the Middle East and ‌Russia," Saxo Bank's head of commodity strategy Ole ⁠Hansen said in a note.

Meanwhile, Reuters reported that Saudi Arabia is planning an offensive against the Houthis in the coming weeks, with options being considered including a coastal push to secure the Red Sea shipping route or an assault on multiple fronts.

Saudi has concluded it cannot enter new Yemeni peace negotiations with the Houthis while the ​militants remain in control of Bab el-Mandeb, the southern exit passage of the Red ​Sea, which gives them significant global leverage, the report said.
Oil prices had moved higher earlier in the week following reports the U.S. was sending a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East, raising the possibility of an impending increase in fighting.
